question: Which lung cancer type is most often managed primarily with surgical resection when detected at early stages?
cited_learning_objective: Know which type(s) of lung cancer are primarily treated with surgery and which almost exclusively with drug therapies (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.rationale: NSCLC is usually resectable in early stages and surgery is the first-line local therapy; would be incorrect if disease were advanced or unresectable.
SCLC is usually widespread at diagnosis and rarely treated primarily with surgery; it would be correct only for extremely rare very limited-stage SCLC.
Diffuse metastatic disease is not managed primarily with surgery; resection would be inappropriate unless solitary metastasis amenable to resection.
Multifocal disease is typically not treated with curative surgery; a single localized lesion would be required to make surgery primary.
Typical carcinoids may be resected but the lecture contrasts NSCLC versus SCLC for primary surgical management; carcinoid is not the tested contrast here.

question: Which regimen is the standard chemotherapy backbone for extensive-stage small cell lung cancer?
cited_learning_objective: Know which drug combinations are used for SCLC vs NSCLC (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.rationale: The lecture lists etoposide + cisplatin (EP) as the standard SCLC regimen; it would be incorrect if a platinum agent were absent.
Carboplatin + paclitaxel is used for NSCLC, not the typical SCLC EP backbone; would be correct for many NSCLC regimens.
Cisplatin + gemcitabine is an NSCLC option, not the canonical SCLC EP regimen; would be correct for non-small cell histology.
Pemetrexed-based regimens and bevacizumab are for non-squamous NSCLC; not standard for SCLC.
Single-agent docetaxel is not the standard first-line SCLC regimen; combination platinum-etoposide is preferred.

question: Which molecular target is directly inhibited by osimertinib in EGFR-mutant NSCLC?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action and targets of each class of the anticancer drugs for treating lung cancer (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.rationale: Osimertinib irreversibly inhibits mutant EGFR (including T790M and L858R); would be incorrect if the target were wild-type EGFR only.
ALK inhibitors target ALK fusions; osimertinib targets EGFR mutants, not ALK.
VEGFR inhibitors (e.g., axitinib) target angiogenesis; osimertinib targets EGFR mutations instead.
PD-1 is targeted by checkpoint inhibitor antibodies like pembrolizumab; osimertinib is a small-molecule EGFR inhibitor.
BRAF inhibitors target V600 mutations; osimertinib does not inhibit BRAF.

question: Which adverse effect is classically associated with platinum-based chemotherapy and may be mitigated by coadministration of amifostine?
cited_learning_objective: List the major adverse effects of the drugs (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.rationale: Platinum compounds cause nephrotoxicity and amifostine is used to lessen platinum nephrotoxicity; would be incorrect if referring to non-platinum toxicities.
Immune checkpoint inhibitors cause pneumonitis; amifostine does not prevent immune-mediated AEs.
EGFR inhibitors cause dermatologic rash; amifostine is not used to prevent this effect.
VEGF blockade impairs wound healing; amifostine is not indicated for this toxicity.
ALK inhibitors can prolong QT; amifostine does not mitigate QT effects.

question: A patient with metastatic NSCLC lacks driver mutations. Which addition to platinum-doublet chemotherapy is commonly used to improve outcomes?
cited_learning_objective: Know which drug combinations are used for SCLC vs NSCLC (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.text: PD-1 or PD-L1 immune checkpoint inhibitor
options.rationale: For driver mutation-negative NSCLC, immunotherapy (PD-1/PD-L1 antibodies) is commonly added to chemotherapy; would be incorrect if a targeted driver were present.
EGFR TKIs are added only when EGFR driver mutations are present; not appropriate for driver-negative disease.
ALK inhibitors are for ALK-positive tumors; they are not added to chemo in ALK-negative patients.
Angiogenesis inhibitors may be used in some settings but the lecture emphasizes immunotherapy as the common add-on for driver-negative NSCLC.
Chronic high-dose steroids are not a standard adjunct to chemotherapy for NSCLC and would worsen immune responses.

question: Which mechanism best explains how PD-1 or PD-L1 monoclonal antibodies enhance antitumor immunity?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action and targets of each class of the anticancer drugs for treating lung cancer (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.text: Block PD-1/PD-L1 interaction to increase T-cell killing
options.rationale: PD-1/PD-L1 antibodies prevent PD-1 activation by PD-L1, restoring T-cell activity against tumor cells; would be incorrect if they directly killed tumor cells without immune mediation.

options.text: Directly alkylate tumor DNA causing apoptosis
options.rationale: Alkylators damage DNA directly; checkpoint antibodies act via immune disinhibition, not DNA alkylation.

options.text: Inhibit VEGF to reduce tumor angiogenesis
options.rationale: VEGF inhibitors target angiogenesis; PD-1/PD-L1 antibodies modulate T-cell responses instead.

options.text: Block CTLA4 to prevent T-cell activation
options.rationale: Blocking CTLA4 increases T-cell activation but is a different checkpoint pathway; PD-1/PD-L1 blockade specifically prevents PD-1 signaling.

options.text: Deliver cytotoxic payload into tumor cells
options.rationale: Antibody-drug conjugates deliver toxins; PD-1/PD-L1 mAbs do not carry cytotoxic payloads.

question: Which adverse effect profile is shared across PD-1, PD-L1, and CTLA4 blocking antibodies?
cited_learning_objective: List the major adverse effects of the drugs (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.rationale: Checkpoint inhibitors cause autoimmune/inflammatory AEs such as pneumonitis, colitis, and thyroiditis; would be incorrect if describing cytotoxic chemo toxicities.
Nephrotoxicity is characteristic of platinum chemotherapy, not the class-wide effect of checkpoint inhibitors.
Peripheral neuropathy is common with platinum and taxanes; checkpoint inhibitors cause immune AEs instead.
Myelosuppression is typical of cytotoxic agents; immune checkpoint blockade does not primarily cause marrow suppression.
These are characteristic of VEGF pathway inhibitors, not checkpoint antibodies.

question: Which drug class produces an acneiform rash that correlates with improved survival in treated patients?
cited_learning_objective: Describe and adverse effects that might indicate drug efficacy (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.rationale: EGFR inhibitors commonly cause acneiform rash and the lecture notes this dermatologic reaction correlates with greater survival; would be incorrect for non-EGFR-targeted classes.
ALK inhibitors have other AEs (QT, visual) but not the characteristic acneiform rash tied to efficacy.
Checkpoint inhibitors cause immune-related AEs but not the specific acneiform rash linked to EGFR inhibition.
Platinum agents cause nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neuropathy, and myelosuppression, not acneiform rash.
VEGF inhibitors cause hemorrhage and impaired wound healing, not the acneiform rash associated with EGFR blockade.

question: A tumor harbors an EML4-ALK fusion. Which drug class is the most appropriate targeted therapy?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action and targets of each class of the anticancer drugs for treating lung cancer (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.rationale: ALK fusions are treated with ALK inhibitors (e.g., crizotinib, alectinib); would be incorrect if the tumor lacked ALK rearrangement.
EGFR TKIs target EGFR mutations, not ALK fusions; they would be appropriate only if EGFR mutation coexisted.
Checkpoint inhibitors are used broadly but targeted ALK inhibitors are preferred when ALK fusion drives disease.
VEGFR inhibitors target angiogenesis, not the oncogenic ALK fusion protein.
BRAF inhibitors target BRAF V600 mutations, not ALK fusions.

question: Which statement best describes the cell-cycle specificity of platinum chemotherapy agents?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action and targets of each class of the anticancer drugs for treating lung cancer (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.rationale: Platinum compounds are non–cell-cycle-specific alkylators that bind DNA (e.g., N7 guanine); would be incorrect if labeled as cell-cycle specific.
Antimetabolites are S-phase specific; platinum agents act across cell cycle phases.
Taxanes and vinca alkaloids target M phase; platinum drugs do not.
Checkpoint kinase inhibitors are a different targeted class; platinum agents alkylate DNA directly.
MEK inhibitors target MAPK signaling; platinum compounds are DNA-damaging agents.

question: A patient with squamous NSCLC develops hypercalcemia due to tumor secretion of PTHrP. Which class of drugs listed in the lecture is appropriate to inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption?
cited_learning_objective: List the major adverse effects of the drugs (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.rationale: The lecture states bisphosphonates (e.g., pamidronate) or denosumab inhibit osteoclast activity for PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia; would be incorrect if osteoclast inhibition were absent.
EGFR TKIs do not directly treat hypercalcemia from PTHrP; they target tumor EGFR signaling.
Checkpoint inhibitors do not directly inhibit osteoclasts and are not first-line for hypercalcemia management.
VEGF inhibitors affect angiogenesis, not osteoclast-mediated bone resorption.
ALK inhibitors target ALK fusion proteins, not bone resorption from PTHrP.

question: Which targeted therapy mechanism involves antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) as part of its antitumor effect?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action and targets of each class of the anticancer drugs for treating lung cancer (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.text: Monoclonal antibodies binding tumor surface receptors
options.rationale: Some mAbs (e.g., necitumumab, amivantamab) bind extracellular tumor receptors and induce ADCC; would be incorrect for small-molecule inhibitors that lack Fc-mediated ADCC.
Small-molecule TKIs inhibit intracellular kinase activity and do not mediate ADCC.
Platinum drugs damage DNA directly and do not trigger ADCC.
MEK inhibitors block intracellular signaling and do not rely on ADCC.
Proteasome inhibitors affect protein degradation pathways and are not ADCC-mediating antibodies.

question: Which adverse effect is specifically noted for ALK inhibitor therapy in the lecture slides?
cited_learning_objective: List the major adverse effects of the drugs (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.rationale: ALK inhibitors are associated with QT prolongation, visual symptoms, GI effects, and myelosuppression per the lecture; would be incorrect if claiming only dermatologic rash.
Nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity are classic for platinum agents, not ALK inhibitors.
Acneiform rash is characteristic of EGFR inhibitors, not ALK inhibitors.
These are VEGF inhibitor toxicities, not typical ALK inhibitor effects.
Immune-mediated colitis is a checkpoint inhibitor toxicity, not an ALK inhibitor AE.

question: A patient with NSCLC has an exon 20 insertion EGFR mutation. Which agent from the lecture is specifically indicated for exon 20 insertion mutants?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action and targets of each class of the anticancer drugs for treating lung cancer (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.rationale: Sunvozertinib is noted for activity against EGFR exon 20 insertion mutants; it would be incorrect if the mutation were exon 19 deletion or L858R where other TKIs apply.
Crizotinib targets ALK, ROS1, and c-MET, not specifically EGFR exon 20 insertions.
Osimertinib targets common EGFR mutants including T790M and L858R but exon 20 insertions are better targeted by agents like sunvozertinib.
Bevacizumab targets VEGF and angiogenesis, not EGFR exon 20 insertion mutations.
Pembrolizumab is a PD-1 inhibitor used for immunotherapy, not a targeted EGFR exon 20 insertion inhibitor.

question: Which drug class listed in the lecture intercepts a ligand by using a fusion protein ending in -cept?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action and targets of each class of the anticancer drugs for treating lung cancer (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.rationale: Drugs ending in -cept (e.g., ziv-aflibercept) are fusion proteins that intercept ligands like VEGF; would be incorrect if describing monoclonal antibodies or TKIs.
mAbs bind targets via antibody structure; -cept fusion proteins specifically intercept ligands rather than acting as conventional antibodies.
Small-molecule inhibitors end in -ib and inhibit kinases intracellularly, not by ligand interception.
Antimetabolites are cytotoxic chemotherapies and are unrelated to -cept fusion proteins.
ADCs deliver cytotoxic payloads via antibodies; -cept proteins act by ligand sequestration.

question: Which targeted therapy approach would be most appropriate for a tumor with a KRAS G12C mutation according to the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action and targets of each class of the anticancer drugs for treating lung cancer (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.rationale: Sotorasib and adagrasib form covalent bonds with KRAS G12C and are indicated for that mutation; would be incorrect if KRAS mutation were a different codon.
BRAF inhibitors target V600 mutations, not KRAS G12C.
EGFR exon 19 deletion TKIs target EGFR mutations, not KRAS G12C.
ALK inhibitors target ALK fusions, not KRAS point mutations.
VEGFR inhibitors target angiogenesis, not oncogenic KRAS G12C.

question: A patient receiving bevacizumab develops a nonhealing surgical wound and hemoptysis. Which mechanism explains these adverse events?
cited_learning_objective: List the major adverse effects of the drugs (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.text: VEGF pathway inhibition impairing angiogenesis and healing
options.rationale: Bevacizumab binds VEGF and inhibits angiogenesis, causing hemorrhage and impaired wound healing; would be incorrect if the drug did not target VEGF.

options.text: Immune checkpoint activation causing autoimmune vasculitis
options.rationale: Immune checkpoint inhibitors cause autoimmune inflammation but bevacizumab's AEs are due to VEGF blockade, not immune activation.

options.text: EGFR blockade causing skin breakdown and secondary bleeding
options.rationale: EGFR inhibitors cause dermatologic toxicity, not impaired wound angiogenesis leading to hemorrhage.
Platinum agents can cause myelosuppression and bleeding risk, but the combination of impaired wound healing and hemorrhage is characteristic of VEGF inhibition.

options.text: ALK inhibitor–related QT prolongation causing mucosal ischemia
options.rationale: QT prolongation does not explain impaired wound healing or hemoptysis; this distractor is a teachable mismatch.

question: A patient with NSCLC has an EGFR L858R mutation and develops diarrhea and hypomagnesemia after starting therapy. Which drug class is most likely responsible?
cited_learning_objective: List the major adverse effects of the drugs (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.rationale: EGFR inhibitors cause dermatologic reactions, diarrhea, and hypomagnesemia per the lecture; would be incorrect if the patient were on a non-EGFR targeted agent.
ALK inhibitors cause QT prolongation and visual symptoms rather than hypomagnesemia and diarrhea as primary AEs.
Checkpoint inhibitors cause immune-mediated AEs like colitis but hypomagnesemia is more characteristic of EGFR TKIs.
Platinum agents cause nephrotoxicity and neuropathy; hypomagnesemia and diarrhea point toward EGFR-targeted therapy.
VEGF inhibitors cause hemorrhage and wound-healing issues, not the specific hypomagnesemia described.

question: Which therapeutic strategy is most appropriate for a patient with NSCLC whose tumor tests positive for ROS1 fusion?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action and targets of each class of the anticancer drugs for treating lung cancer (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.rationale: ROS1 fusions are treated with ROS1 inhibitors (e.g., crizotinib, entrectinib); would be incorrect if ROS1 fusion were absent.
EGFR TKIs target EGFR mutations, not ROS1 fusions; they would be appropriate only if EGFR mutation coexisted.
Some ALK inhibitors also inhibit ROS1, but the correct approach is a ROS1-targeted TKI rather than ALK-only therapy.
Checkpoint inhibitors may be used broadly but targeted ROS1 inhibition is preferred when ROS1 fusion drives disease.
VEGF -cept proteins target angiogenesis, not ROS1 fusion oncogenes.

question: A patient with metastatic NSCLC receives pembrolizumab and later develops new-onset hypothyroidism. Which mechanism explains this adverse event?
cited_learning_objective: List the major adverse effects of the drugs (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.rationale: Checkpoint inhibitors can cause autoimmune thyroiditis leading to hypothyroidism; would be incorrect if the drug were a non-immune-targeted agent.

options.text: Direct thyroid follicular cell alkylation by pembrolizumab
options.rationale: Pembrolizumab does not alkylate DNA; hypothyroidism arises from immune-mediated inflammation, not direct cytotoxicity.
EGFR inhibitors cause dermatologic and GI AEs, not the classic immune-mediated thyroiditis seen with checkpoint inhibitors.
VEGF inhibitors cause vascular AEs but immune-mediated thyroiditis is the mechanism with PD-1 blockade.
Platinum agents cause cytotoxic effects and nephrotoxicity, not immune-mediated thyroiditis typical of checkpoint inhibitors.

question: Which drug from the lecture is a fusion protein that binds VEGF and prevents receptor activation?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action and targets of each class of the anticancer drugs for treating lung cancer (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.rationale: Ziv-aflibercept is a VEGF ligand-trapping fusion protein (-cept) that binds VEGF; would be incorrect if naming a monoclonal antibody instead.
Bevacizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds VEGF, not a fusion -cept protein; both bind VEGF but differ structurally.
Ramucirumab binds VEGFR2 (the receptor), not the ligand via a fusion protein.
Axitinib is a small-molecule VEGFR kinase inhibitor, not a ligand-trapping fusion protein.
Pembrolizumab is a PD-1 antibody and unrelated to VEGF ligand trapping.

question: A patient with advanced NSCLC and an EGFR exon 19 deletion is started on afatinib. Which description best matches afatinib's mechanism?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action and targets of each class of the anticancer drugs for treating lung cancer (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.rationale: Afatinib irreversibly inhibits certain EGFR mutants (exon 19 deletion, L858R, others); would be incorrect if described as reversible.
Reversible extracellular antibodies (e.g., necitumumab) bind EGFR outside the cell; afatinib is an irreversible small-molecule TKI.
ALK inhibitors target ALK fusions; afatinib targets EGFR mutants, not ALK.
Afatinib is not a fusion protein or immune checkpoint agent; this distractor mixes classes.
VEGFR inhibitors target angiogenesis; afatinib targets EGFR signaling directly.

question: Which of the following best explains why some EGFR inhibitor–related skin rashes are considered a favorable sign?
cited_learning_objective: Describe and adverse effects that might indicate drug efficacy (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.text: On-target EGFR inhibition in skin correlates with tumor response
options.rationale: The acneiform rash reflects on-target EGFR blockade in epithelial tissues and correlates with improved survival; would be incorrect if rash were off-target or unrelated to drug activity.

options.text: Immune activation causing paraneoplastic dermatologic improvement
options.rationale: Immune activation from checkpoint inhibitors can cause skin AEs, but the EGFR rash is an on-target effect, not immune-mediated improvement.

options.text: VEGF blockade causing cutaneous ischemia linked to tumor shrinkage
options.rationale: VEGF inhibition causes vascular AEs, not the acneiform rash tied to EGFR inhibition.
Platinum hypersensitivity is not the acneiform rash and does not explain the correlation with EGFR-targeted efficacy.

options.text: Off-target kinase inhibition causing nonspecific inflammation
options.rationale: The lecture attributes the rash to on-target EGFR effects rather than nonspecific off-target inflammation.

question: A patient with SCLC receives etoposide and cisplatin. Which cellular process is primarily targeted by etoposide?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action and targets of each class of the anticancer drugs for treating lung cancer (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.text: Topoisomerase II inhibition causing DNA strand breaks
options.rationale: Etoposide inhibits topoisomerase II leading to DNA breaks and impaired replication; would be incorrect if described as a platinum DNA alkylator.

options.text: DNA cross-linking at N7 guanine by platinum
options.rationale: Cisplatin cross-links DNA at N7 guanine; etoposide acts via topoisomerase II inhibition, not DNA alkylation.
Taxanes stabilize microtubules; etoposide targets topoisomerase II instead.
Checkpoint blockade is immunotherapy and unrelated to etoposide's topoisomerase inhibition.
VEGF sequestration is the mechanism of -cept proteins; etoposide is a topoisomerase inhibitor.

question: Which targeted agent class would be most appropriate for a tumor with RET fusion per the lecture's drug list?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action and targets of each class of the anticancer drugs for treating lung cancer (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.rationale: RET fusions are targeted by RET inhibitors (e.g., selpercatinib, pralsetinib) as listed; would be incorrect if using non-RET-targeted therapy.
EGFR exon 20 inhibitors target EGFR mutations, not RET fusions.
ALK inhibitors target ALK fusions, not RET rearrangements.
KRAS G12C inhibitors target that specific KRAS mutation, not RET fusions.
VEGF -cept proteins target angiogenesis, not RET oncogenic drivers.

question: Which of the following best characterizes antibody-drug conjugates targeting HER2 mentioned in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action and targets of each class of the anticancer drugs for treating lung cancer (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.text: Antibodies bind HER2 and deliver cytotoxic payloads
options.rationale: ADC agents (e.g., ado-trastuzumab emtansine, deruxtecan) bind HER2 and deliver toxins to tumor cells; would be incorrect if claiming they act solely by ADCC.
Some drugs are small-molecule HER2 inhibitors, but ADCs specifically deliver cytotoxic payloads via antibody targeting.
VEGF antibodies target angiogenesis, not HER2-directed ADC cytotoxic delivery.

options.text: Immune checkpoint antibodies enhancing T-cell killing
options.rationale: Checkpoint antibodies modulate immunity; ADCs deliver cytotoxins directly to HER2-expressing cells.

options.text: Ligand-trapping fusion proteins sequestering HER2 ligands
options.rationale: HER2 ADCs are not ligand-trapping fusion proteins; they are antibody conjugates with cytotoxic drugs.

question: A patient with NSCLC has a BRAF V600E mutation. According to the lecture, which combination of inhibitors would be mechanistically appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action and targets of each class of the anticancer drugs for treating lung cancer (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.rationale: BRAF V600 mutations are treated with BRAF inhibitors (vemurafenib, dabrafenib) often combined with MEK inhibitors (trametinib) to block MAPK pathway; would be incorrect if using single-agent unrelated inhibitors.
KRAS G12C inhibitors target a different mutation; they are not appropriate for BRAF V600E tumors.

options.text: EGFR irreversible TKI plus PD-1 antibody
options.rationale: EGFR TKIs target EGFR mutations; combining with PD-1 blockade is not the specific targeted strategy for BRAF V600E.
ALK inhibitors target ALK fusions; this combination does not address BRAF V600E-driven MAPK signaling.

options.text: VEGF ligand trap plus HER2 ADC
options.rationale: These agents target angiogenesis and HER2 respectively, not the BRAF-driven MAPK pathway.

question: Which of the following best explains why platinum compounds cause ototoxicity and peripheral neuropathy in addition to nephrotoxicity?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action and targets of each class of the anticancer drugs for treating lung cancer (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.text: DNA cross-linking damages rapidly dividing and sensitive tissues
options.rationale: Platinum agents covalently bind DNA causing damage that affects dividing cells and sensitive tissues like renal tubular cells, cochlea, and peripheral nerves; would be incorrect if attributing these AEs to immune mechanisms.
Immune-mediated toxicity is characteristic of checkpoint inhibitors, not platinum-induced ototoxicity or neuropathy.

options.text: VEGF inhibition causing ischemic nerve injury
options.rationale: VEGF inhibitors cause vascular AEs but platinum neuropathy and ototoxicity are due to direct cytotoxic effects, not ischemia.

options.text: EGFR blockade causing epidermal sensory loss
options.rationale: EGFR inhibitors cause dermatologic effects; they do not explain platinum-associated neuropathy and ototoxicity.
ALK inhibitors have different toxicity profiles; platinum toxicities are due to DNA damage and related cellular injury.

question: A patient with SCLC is enrolled in a trial of tarlatamab, a bispecific antibody that binds DLL3 on tumor cells and CD3 on T cells. Which mechanism best describes its intended antitumor action?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action and targets of each class of the anticancer drugs for treating lung cancer (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.text: Redirect T cells to kill DLL3-expressing tumor cells
options.rationale: Tarlatamab is a bispecific antibody that binds DLL3 and CD3 to activate T cells against tumor cells; would be incorrect if described as a simple checkpoint inhibitor.

options.text: Block PD-1 to relieve T-cell inhibition
options.rationale: PD-1 blockade relieves inhibition but tarlatamab actively redirects T cells via CD3 engagement, a different mechanism.

options.text: Deliver cytotoxic payload into DLL3-positive cells
options.rationale: Antibody-drug conjugates deliver toxins; tarlatamab functions by T-cell engagement rather than payload delivery.

options.text: Sequester VEGF to inhibit tumor angiogenesis
options.rationale: VEGF sequestration targets angiogenesis and is unrelated to bispecific T-cell engager mechanisms.

options.text: Irreversibly inhibit DLL3 intracellular kinase activity
options.rationale: DLL3 is targeted extracellularly by the bispecific antibody; there is no intracellular kinase inhibition involved.

question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for a patient with advanced NSCLC found to have high PD-L1 expression but no actionable driver mutation?
cited_learning_objective: When are immunotherapies used? Which drugs belong in each class?

options.text: Add PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitor to chemotherapy
options.rationale: For driver-negative NSCLC, immunotherapy (PD-1/PD-L1 antibodies) is commonly added to chemotherapy; would be incorrect if a driver mutation were present requiring targeted therapy.

options.text: Start EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor monotherapy
options.rationale: EGFR TKIs are indicated only with EGFR mutations; high PD-L1 alone does not justify EGFR-targeted therapy.
ALK inhibitors require ALK rearrangement; PD-L1 expression does not indicate ALK positivity.

options.text: Use VEGF ligand trap as sole systemic therapy
options.rationale: VEGF-targeted agents are not standard monotherapy for PD-L1–high, driver-negative NSCLC; immunotherapy is preferred.
Chemotherapy alone is an option, but the lecture emphasizes adding checkpoint inhibitors for driver-negative disease to improve outcomes.

question: Which drug naming infix indicates a monoclonal antibody designed to modulate the immune system (checkpoint inhibitor) as described in the nomenclature slide?
cited_learning_objective: Antineoplastic Drug Nomenclature

options.text: The infix -li- or -lim- within the name
options.rationale: The lecture notes that infixes like -l(i)(m)- indicate immune system targeting (e.g., PD-1/PD-L1 or CTLA4 antibodies); would be incorrect if claiming a different infix.

options.text: The suffix -ib indicating a small-molecule inhibitor
options.rationale: Suffix -ib denotes small-molecule signal transduction inhibitors, not immune-targeting mAbs.

options.text: The prefix indicating the unique antibody name
options.rationale: The prefix is unique but does not indicate immune targeting; the infix conveys target class.
-ci- indicates circulatory/angiogenesis targeting (e.g., VEGF), not immune checkpoint modulation.

options.text: The suffix -cept indicating a fusion protein
options.rationale: -cept denotes fusion proteins that intercept ligands, not immune-targeting monoclonal antibodies.

question: Which of the following best describes why some newer targeted agents are called 'biologics' in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action and targets of each class of the anticancer drugs for treating lung cancer (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.text: They are protein drugs, mostly monoclonal antibodies
options.rationale: The lecture states that protein drugs (mostly mAbs) are known as biologics; would be incorrect if describing small molecules as biologics.
Small molecules are not biologics; biologics are typically protein-based therapies.
Alkylators are chemical cytotoxics, not biologic protein drugs.

options.text: They are fusion proteins that always deliver toxins
options.rationale: Some fusion proteins are biologics, but not all biologics deliver toxins; ADCs deliver payloads, while many biologics act by binding targets.

options.text: They are immune checkpoint small peptides
options.rationale: Checkpoint inhibitors are monoclonal antibodies (proteins), not small peptides; the lecture groups them as biologics.

question: Which of the following is the most likely reason to add amifostine when administering platinum chemotherapy?
cited_learning_objective: Describe any drug treatments to prevent/minimize cancer drug toxicities. (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.text: To scavenge free radicals and reduce nephrotoxicity
options.rationale: Amifostine is a free radical scavenger activated in nonacidic conditions and is coadministered to lessen platinum nephrotoxicity; would be incorrect if used to prevent immune AEs.

options.text: To prevent immune-mediated colitis from checkpoint inhibitors
options.rationale: Amifostine does not prevent immune-related AEs from checkpoint blockade; immunosuppression or steroids are used instead.
Amifostine does not treat EGFR inhibitor dermatologic toxicity; topical or dose modification strategies are used.

options.text: To block VEGF and reduce bleeding risk
options.rationale: Amifostine does not inhibit VEGF; it protects normal tissues from free radical damage, particularly renal.

options.text: To chelate platinum and increase tumor uptake
options.rationale: Amifostine does not chelate platinum to increase tumor uptake; it protects normal tissues from toxicity.

question: Which of the following best summarizes when targeted therapies are preferred over conventional chemotherapy in NSCLC?
cited_learning_objective: Know which drug combinations are used for SCLC vs NSCLC (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.text: When a tumor harbors a specific actionable driver mutation
options.rationale: Targeted therapies are used when driver mutations (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, RET, etc.) are present; would be incorrect if no actionable mutation exists.

options.text: For all advanced NSCLC regardless of mutation status
options.rationale: Targeted therapy requires an actionable mutation; immunotherapy or chemotherapy are used when drivers are absent.

options.text: Only after failure of platinum-doublet chemotherapy
options.rationale: Targeted agents are often first-line when a driver mutation is identified, not reserved only after chemo failure.
Some targeted therapies are more common in non-squamous NSCLC; squamous histology is not the sole indication.
PD-L1 expression guides immunotherapy use; targeted therapy depends on driver mutations, not PD-L1 level.

question: Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation if a patient on an EGFR inhibitor develops a prominent acneiform rash early in therapy?
cited_learning_objective: Describe and adverse effects that might indicate drug efficacy (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.text: On-target effect that may correlate with better tumor response
options.rationale: The lecture notes that dermatologic reactions from EGFR inhibitors correlate with greater survival, indicating an on-target effect; would be incorrect if rash were assumed to indicate treatment failure.

options.text: Immediate drug hypersensitivity requiring permanent discontinuation
options.rationale: While severe hypersensitivity may require stopping therapy, the typical acneiform rash is an expected on-target AE and not an automatic reason for permanent discontinuation.

options.text: VEGF inhibitor toxicity signaling bleeding risk
options.rationale: VEGF inhibitors cause bleeding and wound-healing issues, not acneiform rash associated with EGFR inhibitors.
Platinum ototoxicity affects hearing, not causing acneiform skin eruptions; this distractor conflates unrelated toxicities.

options.text: Immune checkpoint–related dermatitis indicating autoimmune activation
options.rationale: Checkpoint inhibitors can cause immune dermatitis, but the acneiform rash described is characteristic of EGFR blockade and is on-target rather than autoimmune.

question: Which of the following best describes the role of angiogenesis inhibitors in lung cancer therapy per the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action and targets of each class of the anticancer drugs for treating lung cancer (AACOM competency II.1.f)

options.text: They inhibit VEGF signaling to reduce tumor blood vessel formation
options.rationale: Angiogenesis inhibitors (bevacizumab, ramucirumab, VEGFR TKIs) block VEGF/VEGFR signaling to inhibit tumor angiogenesis; would be incorrect if claiming they directly kill tumor cells.

options.text: They directly alkylate tumor DNA causing cell death
options.rationale: Alkylators like platinum compounds damage DNA; angiogenesis inhibitors act on vascular signaling, not DNA.

options.text: They activate T cells by blocking PD-1
options.rationale: Checkpoint inhibitors activate T cells; angiogenesis inhibitors target VEGF pathways instead.
EGFR inhibitors target epithelial growth signaling, not angiogenesis mediated by VEGF.

options.text: They sequester HER2 ligands to prevent receptor activation
options.rationale: HER2-targeted therapies act on HER2; angiogenesis inhibitors target VEGF/VEGFR signaling.
